quiz_ly:10.q: The deep clefts running into this organ are lined by which epithelium?
quiz_ly:10.r: Palatine tonsil crypts: non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
quiz_ly:10.alt: Low-power micrograph of an oval lymphoid organ with deep clefts

quiz_ly:11.q: Antigen is carried across the epithelium overlying these nodules by which cell?
quiz_ly:11.r: Peyer's patch (villi = small intestine): M cells transport antigen.
quiz_ly:11.alt: Micrograph of nodules beneath finger-like projections

quiz_ly:14.q: Which feature distinguishes the organ shown from a Peyer's patch?
quiz_ly:14.r: Appendix: nodules below crypts, no villi (faculty slide 558 logic).
quiz_ly:14.alt: Cross-section of a small tubular organ with a narrow lumen

quiz_ly:15.q: These sections show the same organ at ages 10 and 36. Which change with age do they illustrate?
quiz_ly:15.r: Appendix lymphoid tissue atrophies progressively with age.
quiz_ly:15.alt: Two cross-sections of a tubular organ labeled 10 yoa and 36 yoa

quiz_ly:16.q: A newborn in whom the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches failed to develop lacks the organ shown. Which cells will be deficient?
quiz_ly:16.r: DiGeorge: no thymus, no T cells. Thymus = lobules with dark cortex, pale medulla.
quiz_ly:16.alt: Micrograph of an organ divided into lobules with dark rims and pale centers

quiz_ly:17.q: The capillary shown is sealed by a thick basal lamina and a sleeve of epithelial cells, so developing lymphocytes meet no foreign antigen. In which region is this barrier found?
quiz_ly:17.alt: Electron micrograph of a capillary surrounded by cells

quiz_ly:18.q: What is the function of the structure labeled H?
quiz_ly:18.r: Hassall's corpuscle: medullary epithelial origin, keratinized, secretes thymic epithelial cytokines.
quiz_ly:18.alt: Micrograph with a whorled pink structure labeled H

quiz_ly:23.q: By which route do most lymphocytes enter the organ shown?
quiz_ly:23.r: Lymph node: HEV are the main route of lymphocyte entry.
quiz_ly:23.alt: Low-power micrograph of an oval encapsulated organ

quiz_ly:24.q: This postcapillary venule with a cuboidal endothelium is found in which region of a lymph node?
quiz_ly:24.r: HEV are in the paracortex (T-cell area).
quiz_ly:24.alt: Drawing of a small vessel with tall lining cells

quiz_ly:25.q: Which cells in the region labeled medulla secrete antibody into the efferent lymph?
quiz_ly:25.r: Lymph node medullary cords: plasma cells secrete antibody into efferent lymph.
quiz_ly:25.alt: Low-power micrograph of an oval organ with labels medulla, cortex and germinal centers

quiz_ly:28.q: Within the areas labeled white pulp, where are T cells concentrated?
quiz_ly:28.r: PALS = T cells around the central artery; nodules = B cells.
quiz_ly:28.alt: Micrograph with arrows labeled red pulp and white pulp

quiz_ly:29.q: The image shows the slits in the wall of a venous sinusoid of the spleen. Red cells that cannot deform to pass through are removed by which cells?
quiz_ly:29.r: Non-deformable cells stay in the splenic cords and are phagocytosed by macrophages.
quiz_ly:29.alt: Scanning electron micrograph of a slatted vessel wall

quiz_ly:3.q: Plasma cells in the regions labeled LP mainly secrete which immunoglobulin?
quiz_ly:3.r: Lamina propria plasma cells secrete IgA.
quiz_ly:3.alt: Light micrograph of intestinal villi and crypts with letter labels

quiz_ly:30.q: About what share of blood flow through the red pulp takes the slow, open route used for filtration?

quiz_ly:4.q: The cells labeled P at the base of the crypts secrete which product?
quiz_ly:4.alt: Light micrograph of intestinal villi and crypts with letter labels

quiz_ly:5.q: The secretory piece of immunoglobulin A is added by which cells?
quiz_ly:5.r: Plasma cells make the IgA dimer; epithelial cells add the secretory piece during transcytosis.

quiz_ly:7.q: The region labeled M consists mainly of which cells?
quiz_ly:7.alt: Light micrograph of a mucosal nodule with regions labeled M and G

quiz_ly:8.q: The organ shown belongs to which class of lymphoid tissue?
quiz_ly:8.r: Palatine tonsil: aggregated nodules, incompletely encapsulated.
quiz_ly:8.alt: Low-power micrograph of a lobed lymphoid organ

quiz_ly_b:1.q: Which fluid does this organ survey for antigen, and is the organ encapsulated?
quiz_ly_b:1.r: A capsule with nodules in the cortex beneath it marks a lymph node (p. 1178). On the organization slide the encapsulated peripheral organs are lymph nodes, which survey lymph, and the spleen, which surveys blood; MALT is unencapsulated and surveys mucosal surfaces (p. 510).
quiz_ly_b:1.alt: Low-power section of the edge of a lymphoid organ with round nodules lying just under its outer covering.

quiz_ly_b:2.q: If mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue holds the share stated on the slide, about what share of all lymphoid tissue is left for every other site combined?
quiz_ly_b:2.r: MALT houses 85% of all lymphoid tissue, which leaves about 15% for everything else; this is why MALT is the answer to the lecturer's own question on where most lymphoid tissue lies (p. 510, p. 554).

quiz_ly_b:3.q: Circulating lymphocytes fall into T cells, B cells and natural killer (NK) cells. Which order runs from most to least common on the slide?
o: T cells, B cells, NK cells
B cells, T cells, NK cells
NK cells, T cells, B cells
T cells, NK cells, B cells
B cells, NK cells, T cells
quiz_ly_b:3.r: Circulating lymphocytes are 75% T cells, 15% natural killer cells and 10% B cells, so B cells are the least common (p. 515).

quiz_ly_b:4.q: In which part of the gut is the lymphoid tissue shown here most common?
quiz_ly_b:4.r: Villi place this in the small intestine, and aggregated nodules beneath villi are Peyer's patches, which the slides place in the ileum (p. 525, p. 1162).
quiz_ly_b:4.alt: Low-power section of gut wall with finger-like projections above a row of large round lymphoid nodules.

quiz_ly_b:5.q: Where is the surface landmark for the organ shown, according to the slide?
o: One third of the way from hip to umbilicus
Two thirds of the way from hip to umbilicus
One third of the way from pubis to umbilicus
quiz_ly_b:5.r: Crypts and a lymph nodule with no villi mark the appendix (p. 530), the narrowed tip of the cecum; McBurney's point lies one third of the distance from the hip to the umbilicus (p. 528).
quiz_ly_b:5.alt: Section of gut wall with labelled crypts, mucosa, submucosa and a lymph nodule.

quiz_ly_b:6.q: About what share of the lymphocytes developing in this organ are destroyed before they can leave it?
quiz_ly_b:6.r: Lobules with a dark cortex and pale medulla mark the thymus (p. 1164). The key point on thymic function is that 95% of developing thymocytes are destroyed during selection (p. 537).
quiz_ly_b:6.alt: Low-power section of a lobulated organ; each lobule has a dark outer zone and a paler centre, with fat at the surface.

quiz_ly_b:7.q: From which cells is the arrowed structure derived?
o: Maturing T lymphocytes of the medulla
quiz_ly_b:7.r: The whorled body is a Hassall's corpuscle, unique to the thymus, keratinized and derived from medullary epithelial reticular cells (p. 539; aged epithelial reticular cells on p. 1165).
quiz_ly_b:7.alt: High-power field of small dark cells with several pink whorled bodies; an arrow marks one of them.

quiz_ly_b:8.q: The black fibers in this silver-stained lymph node form its scaffold. What forms the microframework of each lobule in the thymus instead?
quiz_ly_b:8.r: Lymph nodes are filled with argyrophilic reticular cells and fibers (type III collagen) that form the scaffold (p. 545, p. 1167), whereas each thymic lobule has a microframework of epithelial reticular cells (p. 536).
quiz_ly_b:8.alt: Silver-stained section with a dense band of black fibers at one side and a loose black meshwork across the rest.

quiz_ly_b:9.q: Besides its filtering and immune roles, which function does the slide list for this organ?
quiz_ly_b:9.r: Red pulp with islands of white pulp marks the spleen (p. 1177). Its listed functions are filtering blood, the immune response to blood-borne antigen, platelet storage and extra-medullary hematopoiesis; the lecturer marks 'produce platelets' as wrong for the spleen (p. 548, p. 555).
quiz_ly_b:9.alt: Low-power section of an organ with scattered blue-purple islands in a pink-red background.

quiz_ly_recheck:11.q: Which structure is the source of thymic epithelial cytokines?
quiz_ly_recheck:11.r: Hassall's corpuscle: medullary, keratinized, secretes thymic epithelial cytokines.

quiz_ly_recheck:2.q: Resting naive B cells form which part of a secondary lymphoid nodule?

quiz_ly_recheck:5.q: The antibody that protects mucosal surfaces is released by plasma cells as a dimer and receives a secretory piece from epithelial cells. Which antibody is it?
quiz_ly_recheck:5.r: IgA: dimer from lamina propria plasma cells, secretory piece added by epithelial cells.

quiz_ly_recheck:6.q: Which cell samples antigen from the gut lumen and delivers it to the lymphoid cells beneath?
quiz_ly_recheck:6.r: M (microfold) cells transport antigen across the epithelium.

brief:
Lymphoid Organs High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Lymphoid Organs (Djakiew) was 25/43 on your September quiz, with the thymus the weakest part at 2/10. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 508–560, handout pp. 561–578. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides).

1. Organization of the lymphoid system (LO 1)

There are two central organs and everything else is peripheral; mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) houses 85% of all lymphoid tissue (pp. 510, 561).

Class Members Role
Central organ Thymus Makes T cells
Central organ Bone marrow Makes B cells
Peripheral, encapsulated Lymph nodes Surveys lymph
Peripheral, encapsulated Spleen Surveys blood
Peripheral, unencapsulated MALT: single, diffuse, transitory, aggregated Surveys mucosal surfaces

The tissues in order of increasing complexity (p. 512):

  1. Circulating lymphocytes
  2. Diffuse lymphoid tissue
  3. Solitary nodules
  4. Aggregated nodules, incompletely encapsulated: tonsils, Peyer's patches, vermiform appendix
  5. Specific organs, encapsulated: bone marrow, thymus, lymph nodes, spleen
Circulating lymphocyte Share of blood lymphocytes Detail (pp. 515, 563)
T cells 75% CD4+ helper 60%, CD8+ suppressor/cytotoxic 30%
B cells 10%
Null cells 15% Natural killer cells, stem cells

Blood holds only about 2% of the body's lymphocytes, and 1–2% of the pool recirculates every hour (pp. 561, 563).

Homing term Meaning Page
Homing Lymphocyte integrins bind vascular addressins on high endothelial venules 511, 561
Naive lymphocytes Migrate through all peripheral lymphoid tissues 563
Memory and effector lymphocytes Restricted to tissue-selective areas; the only ones that enter skin, joints and lung 563
Ecotaxis Segregation into B-cell and T-cell areas inside a lymphoid structure; controlled by chemokines 563
T-cell rich Same as thymus dependent 563
Immune privileged sites Why (p. 563)
Eye, testis, brain Blood-tissue barriers
No efferent lymphatic drainage
Constitutive expression of Fas ligand
Reduced expression of MHC molecules

MHC is the major histocompatibility complex. Lymphatics are absent from the central nervous system, bone marrow, eyeball, adrenal cortex and inner ear (p. 565).

Two more numbers he stresses: 70–80% of all plasma cells are in the intestines (p. 563), and lymph is one-way, so it does not circulate (p. 563). In evolution, loose unencapsulated tissue came first, encapsulated organs next, and bone last (p. 513).

2. Diffuse tissue, IgA and nodules (LO 3, 5)

Diffuse lymphoid tissue sits in the lamina propria of mucosae and its main product is immunoglobulin A (IgA) (pp. 517, 565).

Diffuse lymphoid tissue Detail Page
Where Lamina propria of respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital mucosa 565
Cells Lymphocytes (mostly B), plasma cells, eosinophils 517
Intraepithelial lymphocytes CD8 and gamma-delta T cells 565
Paneth cells Epithelial cells in the crypts; secrete lysozyme 517

How IgA reaches the lumen (pp. 518, 565):

  1. Plasma cells in the lamina propria release IgA as a dimer
  2. Epithelial cells add the secretory piece during transcytosis
  3. The secretory piece protects the IgA against lysosomal degradation
  4. The piece is clipped at the surface and the IgA dimer is released into the lumen

IgA prevents pathogens colonizing mucosal membranes and neutralizes toxins and viruses (p. 565).

Nodule What it contains State Page
Primary Mainly naive B cells Resting, not stimulated 520, 565
Secondary: mantle (cap) Resting naive B cells; stains dark Periphery of a stimulated nodule 520, 565
Secondary: germinal center B cells, helper T cells, follicular dendritic cells, macrophages with tingible bodies; stains pale Site of B-cell activation, proliferation and differentiation 520, 565

Nodules are unencapsulated, B-cell rich, and lie in the mucosa and submucosa of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urinary tracts and the vagina. A nodule is not a lymph node; nodes are encapsulated (pp. 520, 565).

Germinal center zone Cell What happens there (p. 565)
Dark zone Centroblasts Somatic hypermutation
Light zone Centrocytes Clonal selection: higher antigen affinity

The other germinal center activities are clonal expansion, class (isotype) switching, and generating effector and memory cells. The B cell leaves toward the mantle as an immunoblast and becomes a plasma cell or a memory cell (p. 565).

3. Aggregated nodules: tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix (LO 2, 4)

The tonsils form a discontinuous ring of lymphatic tissue around the entrance of the mouth and nose into the pharynx (pp. 523, 567).

Tonsil Location Surface epithelium Crypts
Palatine Junction of oral cavity and oropharynx Stratified squamous, non-keratinized Several
Pharyngeal (adenoid) Roof of the pharynx Respiratory epithelium None; pleats instead
Lingual Base of the tongue Stratified squamous One each
Tubal Near the pharyngeal opening of the Eustachian tube

The palatine tonsil is incompletely encapsulated (p. 523). The slide calls the pharyngeal tonsil the nasopharyngeal tonsil (p. 522).

Peyer's patch fact Detail Page
Where Lamina propria of the small intestine, especially the ileum 525, 567
Side of the gut Anti-mesenteric side 567
Number About 30, visible to the naked eye 567
M (microfold) cell Domed epithelial cell that samples antigen and delivers it to underlying macrophages and lymphocytes 526, 567
Why M cells matter Major route of antigen transport across the epithelium for the secretory immune response 567
Origin of M cells Formed from enterocytes under the influence of B lymphocytes 567
Agents carried by M cells Polio virus, vibrio, cryptosporidia, HIV 577
Appendix fact Detail Page
Where Terminal narrowed tip of the cecum 528, 567
Nodules Large-intestine wall, below the crypts of Lieberkühn 528
Distinguishing feature Wealth of lymphatic nodules 567
With age Lymphoid tissue atrophies until it almost disappears 529, 567
McBurney's point One third of the distance from the hip to the umbilicus 528
To tell them apart Look for Source
Tonsil Crypt lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium Faculty question, p. 559
Peyer's patch Villi above the nodules, which means small intestine Faculty question, p. 558
Appendix Crypts but no villi, with nodules around a small lumen pp. 528–530, 558

4. Thymus (LO 3–5)

The thymus is the central organ where thymocytes mature into T cells, and 95% of developing thymocytes are destroyed there (pp. 537, 569).

Thymus fact Detail Page
Shape and type Bilobed, lymphoepithelial 534, 569
Position Rests on the pericardium in the superior mediastinum 534, 569
Origin Epithelium of the third pharyngeal pouch, plus lymphoid stem cells from the blood 569
Maturation time About 3 weeks 569
Output Mature T cells that are either CD4+ or CD8+ 569
Epithelial reticular cell job Detail (pp. 536, 569)
Framework Physical microframework of every lobule, cortex and medulla
Hormones Secretes thymosin and interleukins that support T-cell development
Barrier Helps form the blood-thymus barrier, in the cortex only
Epithelial features Desmosomes, cytokeratin filaments, keratohyaline granules
Selection step Also called What happens Who controls it
Positive selection MHC restriction Cells that respect self-MHC are expanded; MHC I selects CD8 cells, MHC II selects CD4 cells Cortical epithelial cells presenting MHC
Negative selection Self tolerance Self-attacking T cells are removed by clonal deletion through apoptosis Cortico-medullary antigen-presenting cells, such as dendritic cells, presenting self-antigen
Feature Cortex Medulla
Lymphocytes Dense, small thymocytes Fewer but larger, maturing
Direction of travel Outer cortex toward medulla as they differentiate
Blood-thymus barrier Present Absent
Macrophages Phagocytose dying lymphocytes (tingible bodies)
Hassall's corpuscle Absent Present
Page 538, 569 539, 569

The blood-thymus barrier is continuous capillaries with a thick basal lamina, surrounded by epithelial reticular cells. It lets thymocytes proliferate free of foreign antigens (p. 569).

Hassall's corpuscle Detail (pp. 539, 569)
Found Thymic medulla only; unique to the thymus
Derived from Medullary epithelial reticular cells
Appearance Keratinized
Function Source of thymic epithelial cytokines
Involution type Cause What changes Page
Aging Begins after puberty, when the thymus is at its greatest weight Lymphocyte depletion and fatty infiltration; under 15% of maximum weight by age 50 541, 571
Acute stress Severe disease, through corticosteroid hormones Rapid loss of cortical thymocytes 571, 577
Compartment Location With involution (p. 571)
Thymopoietic Intraepithelial: cortex and medulla Decreases
Perivascular Extraepithelial: subcapsular space Increases, with fat and mature lymphocytes

Immunosenescence is the immune decline of aging that thymic involution may contribute to (pp. 541, 571).

5. Lymph node (LO 3–5)

A lymph node filters lymph and holds T and B cells for antigen recognition (pp. 544, 571).

Region Main cell Antigen-presenting cell Other Page
Cortex: follicles B cells Follicular dendritic cells, in germinal centers Primary and secondary follicles 545, 571
Paracortex (deep cortex) T cells Interdigitating dendritic cells High endothelial venules are here 545–546, 571
Medulla B cells Plasma cells in medullary cords secrete antibody into efferent lymph 545, 571

Lymph flows through the node in this order (p. 573):

  1. Afferent lymphatics
  2. Subcapsular sinus
  3. Trabecular sinus
  4. Medullary sinus
  5. Efferent lymphatics
Lymph node fact Detail Page
Scaffold Reticular cells and fibers; argyrophilic 545
Sinuses Criss-crossed by reticular fibers, which slow the lymph so macrophages can phagocytose debris and microbes 573
Filtering Removes 99% of lymph debris 571
High endothelial venule Postcapillary venule with cuboidal endothelium; the main route of lymphocyte entry 546, 573
Stay 6–16 hours unless the lymphocyte meets its antigen; it leaves by the efferent lymphatics 573
Number More than 500 nodes 543, 571
Rich sites Neck, mediastinum, retroperitoneum, base of the extremities 543, 571
After antigen Can reach 15 times its size in 5–10 days 577
Cancer Biopsied for metastasis; breast cancer in four or more nodes carried the highest 15-year risk of return 543

6. Spleen (LO 3–5)

The spleen is to blood as the lymph nodes are to lymph (p. 573).

Spleen fact Detail Page
Size Largest single mass of lymphatic tissue in the body 573
Position Left upper quadrant of the abdomen 573
Blood supply Arterial from the systemic circulation; venous drainage into the portal circulation 573
Capsule and trabeculae Contain some smooth muscle and elastic fibers, allowing limited contraction and expansion 573
Function Detail Page
Filters blood Especially old and damaged red cells; also microbes 548, 573
Immune response To blood-borne antigens 548, 573
Platelet storage Up to 33% of all blood platelets 573
Hematopoiesis Normal in the fetus; extramedullary in the adult 548, 573
Region Made of Role Page
White pulp: periarterial lymphatic sheath (PALS) T cells around a central artery T-cell area 511, 575
White pulp: lymphoid nodules B cells B-cell area 575
Marginal zone Between white and red pulp Sorts incoming blood cells, by radial branches of the central arteries 575
Red pulp: splenic cords (cords of Billroth) Reticular cell and fiber meshwork Red cell destruction; platelet and iron storage; plasma cells; hematopoietic stem cells 550, 575
Red pulp: splenic sinusoids Endothelial cells separated by slits of 1–3 microns Only deformable, healthy cells squeeze back into the blood 553, 575

The white pulp is the analog of the lymph node cortex (p. 573).

Blood takes this path (p. 575):

  1. Central artery
  2. Penicillar arterioles
  3. Splenic cords
  4. Venous sinuses
Circulation Purpose Speed Share (pp. 552, 575)
Open Filtration Slow 90%
Closed Nutrition Fast 10%

7. Master tables: where the cells live and how to spot each organ (LO 2–4)

Every peripheral organ has the same split: nodules or follicles are B-cell areas, and the tissue around a vessel or deep to the follicles is the T-cell area.

Organ B-cell area T-cell area Page
Lymph node Cortical follicles; medulla Paracortex 545, 571
Spleen Lymphoid nodules of white pulp Periarterial lymphatic sheath 575
Any nodule Mantle (naive B cells) and germinal center Helper T cells inside the germinal center 520, 565
Gut lamina propria Lymphocytes (mostly B) and IgA plasma cells Intraepithelial T cells 517, 565
Thymus Whole organ: thymocytes in cortex, maturing T cells in medulla 569
Bone marrow Central organ for B cells Also holds plasma cells and T cells as a peripheral organ; a major source of serum antibody 567

His ecotaxis slide adds the fluids: blood and thoracic duct lymph are mostly T cells, while mucosal tissues are mostly B cells (p. 511).

Antigen-presenting cell Where
Follicular dendritic cell Germinal centers
Interdigitating dendritic cell Paracortex of the lymph node
Dendritic cell Cortico-medullary junction of the thymus, for negative selection
Organ Capsule Feature that identifies it Page
Palatine tonsil Incomplete Crypts lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium 523, 559
Peyer's patch None Nodules under small-intestine villi 525, 558
Appendix None Ring of nodules below crypts; no villi 528, 558
Thymus Complete, with trabeculae and lobules Dark cortex, pale medulla, Hassall's corpuscles; no nodules 536, 539
Lymph node Complete Subcapsular sinus, cortical follicles, paracortex, medullary cords and sinuses 545, 557
Spleen Complete, with trabeculae White pulp around central arteries, set in red pulp; no cortex and medulla 549–550

"No nodules" for the thymus and "no cortex and medulla" for the spleen are my shorthand from the slide images, not his wording.

8. Clinical context

These are the handout's clinical notes, each tied to the structure it tests (p. 577).

Condition or fact Mechanism Structure it tests
IgA in breast milk against gut antigens IgA-committed cells home to distant MALT sites, including the lactating mammary gland MALT homing
X-linked agammaglobulinemia Block in pre-B to B cell maturation in bone marrow; no primary or secondary follicles Bone marrow, follicles
Acute stress Corticosteroids kill cortical thymocytes; thymus shrinks Thymic cortex
DiGeorge syndrome Third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail; no thymus, no T cells Thymus origin
Malaria Infected red cells lose deformability and are filtered out Splenic sinusoids
Splenectomy Serious bacterial infections (mortality up to 50–80%); more circulating platelets and aged red cells Spleen functions
Portal hypertension, as in cirrhosis Blood congestion enlarges the spleen Portal venous drainage
M-cell transport Polio virus, vibrio, cryptosporidia and HIV cross here Peyer's patch
AIDS Peripheral CD4 count falls; follicular dendritic cell network degenerates Germinal centers
MALT lymphoma Spreads to other mucosal sites MALT homing
Hodgkin's disease Reed-Sternberg cells, from transformed germinal center B cells Germinal centers
Lymph node that fails to destroy what it traps Becomes a new focus of infection or cancer Lymph node filtering
Fetal immunity By week 20 the fetus can mount T and B cell responses Peripheral organs

9. Faculty questions on the slides, and your September misses

The six practice questions at the end of the slides are faculty-written (pp. 554–559). Two of them ask the function of an organ shown in an image, which is the second-order style you described.

Slide What it asked Answer on the slide
554 Which accounts for most of the lymphoid tissue in the body MALT
555 Major function of the organ shown Remove aged erythrocytes (spleen)
556 Major function of the organ shown Produce T cells (thymus)
557 Identify the organ shown Lymph node
558 Name the tissue shown Peyer's patches; villi mean small intestine, so not appendix
559 Identify the tissue shown Tonsils; crypt lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium

The slide 556 key is printed as "T (thymus)", which is a typo for D, Produce T cells.

Area The fact you missed in September Page
Thymus The blood-thymus barrier is in the cortex only 569
Thymus The epithelial reticular network secretes thymosin and interleukins 569
Thymus Hassall's corpuscle is the source of thymic epithelial cytokines 539
Thymus MHC I selects CD8+ cells 569
Thymus Negative selection removes cells by apoptosis (clonal deletion) 569
Thymus Involution enlarges the perivascular compartment with fat and mature lymphocytes 571
Thymus Stress involution: high corticosteroids kill cortical thymocytes 577
Thymus The thymus's function is to produce T cells 556
Lymph node Paracortex is the T-cell area 571
Lymph node Follicular dendritic cells are the germinal center antigen-presenting cells 571
Lymph node High endothelial venules are the main route of lymphocyte entry 573
Lymph node Criss-crossing reticular fibers slow the lymph in the sinuses 573
Nodules The dark zone is where somatic hypermutation happens 565
Nodules The pharyngeal tonsil has respiratory epithelium and pleats 567
Nodules Peyer's patches concentrate on the anti-mesenteric side of the ileum 567
Nodules M cells form from enterocytes under B-cell influence 567
Spleen White pulp is the analog of the lymph node cortex 573
Spleen The marginal zone sorts incoming blood cells 575

One more from the review quiz: the primary (central) lymphoid organs are the thymus and bone marrow (p. 510).
